template.md lines 8-11: a postmortem describes what system and process allowed, not who erred; people who fear blame hide what they know and the team learns less; write 'a config commit went straight into the Deployment', not 'X changed the config'.

template.md l.35-38: usually several contributing factors, not one root cause; each with what was allowed and why it seemed reasonable then. L.48-55: action items with kind (prevent, detect, mitigate), owner by role, due date, status, in the backlog; closed when all done.

delivery-metrics.md l.29-43: postmortems in docs/postmortems/ record failures not fixed by revert (e.g. a setting changed on the cluster), which git log cannot see; timelines hold deploy and restore times; without them change failure rate reads lower.

People who expect blame hide what they know; asking what the system allowed yields changes the team can make (steps, checks, written rules), while naming a person leaves the conditions in place, so the next person can make the same change.

Trade-offs: blameless fits every incident over the budget threshold and smaller ones worth learning from; naming who never fits as a team practice; no written review fits only when little budget is spent and nothing new is learned. Several factors -> more action items, harder repeat.

Choices: small repeat incident -> optional short postmortem to learn why earlier actions did not stop it (a repeat can mean one is open or incomplete); fix by hand on the cluster -> write at least the timeline since git log cannot see it; open actions at sprint end -> keep open and plan next sprint.
